content: 1. The maximum allowable limits for relevant impurities in manufacturing should be set at less than 1 g/kg. These limits must be supported by analytical data from at least five typical production batches, and the proposer must provide a rationale for these limits, which may include confidential information. 2. Detailed information on relevant impurities, including their observed effects (e.g., toxicological effects or impacts on the stability of the active ingredient), must be provided. Limits established by the FAO/WHO Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR) or other regulatory authorities should accompany this information, with clear identification of the responsible authority. 3. In some cases, impurities that could become relevant at higher concentrations have been identified in technical materials. However, strict control of manufacturing conditions ensures these impurities remain at levels that render them non-relevant. It is noted that such impurities may occur at higher concentrations in materials from other manufacturers. 4. A footnote is added to the technical concentrate (TC) or technical material (TK) specification in cases where impurities could occur at higher concentrations, and the proposer must provide FAO and/or WHO with a validated analytical method for determining the impurity upon request. 5. Analytical methods for relevant impurities must be properly validated, though peer validation is not required. These methods should be included in the specification, while other impurities, including isomers with low activity, should not be included. 6. The identity and nominal content (g/kg) of compounds intentionally added to the TC/TK must be disclosed, even if this information is confidential. 7. Toxicological summaries, including test conditions and results, must be provided. Recent studies must comply with Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) standards and established study guidelines. 8. The toxicological profile of the TC/TK must include data on acute oral, dermal, and inhalation toxicity, as well as skin and eye irritation and skin sensitization. 9. The toxicological profile must also include data from repeated administration studies (ranging from sub-acute to chronic), reproductive and developmental toxicity studies, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, and neurotoxicity (both developmental and adult). 10. Environmental toxicity data, as appropriate to the intended use (e.g., effects on fish, crustaceans, algae, birds, bees), and information on persistence must be provided. 11. References to JMPR or JECFA evaluations for toxicology and environmental fate should be included where available. Toxicological data submitted to JMPR for evaluation must be cross-referenced to the batch analysis data of the technical materials used in those studies. 12. A letter of authorization must be provided, granting FAO/WHO and registration authorities access to registration data to assess whether the technical material proposed for FAO/WHO specification is equivalent to that registered by the authority. 13. If the data submitted to FAO/WHO differ from those submitted for registration, the relevance of the data provided to FAO/WHO must be explained. 14. At the request of FAO/WHO, the proposer may provide a written undertaking that the data submitted to FAO/WHO are identical to those submitted for registration to a specified national authority. Any deviations must be described in detail. 15. Statements must identify the links between purity/impurity data and hazard information and risk assessments. Normally, data provided are expected to have been generated from the proposer’s material. 16. If hazard data were not generated from the proposer’s technical grade active ingredient or formulated products, the source of the information must be stated, and the relevance of the data must be explained. 17. The proposer must identify whether the formulations are intended for public health or agricultural uses, or both. 18. For public health pesticides, the proposer must confirm that the formulation and manufacturing process are the same as those evaluated by WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) for efficacy. 19. The main formulation types available must be listed, and those for which specifications are sought must be identified. 20. The main countries where these formulations are registered and sold must be listed, or if there are many, the number of countries in each region or continent must be provided. 21. Physical properties, as required by sections 5 to 9 of the Manual, must be provided. If necessary, the proposer should explain why certain clauses should be deleted, new clauses inserted, or less stringent limits adopted compared to those in the guideline specifications. 22. At least two methods for testing the identity of the active ingredient and one for testing the identity of the counter-ion or other derivative, if appropriate, must be provided. 23. A method for determining the active ingredient content must be included. If the method has not yet been validated by CIPAC or AOAC, or for the particular formulation, the expected year of validation completion must be indicated. 24. Methods of analysis for relevant impurities must be detailed, including validation data if not published. The principle of the methods used for non-relevant impurities in the TC/TK (e.g., GC with FID) must also be provided. 25. Reference test methods for physical properties must be included. If a method intended for testing compliance with the specification has not yet been validated by CIPAC or for the particular formulation, the expected year of validation completion must be indicated. 26. Methods required to assess compliance with a specification must be independently validated and made publicly available. Specifications will not normally be published before the completion of method validation. 27. Any impurity capable of creating an adverse effect beyond that of the active ingredient is potentially relevant and may need to be controlled by the specification. Adverse effects may reflect toxic or non-toxic hazards. 28. The relevance of an impurity is not determined solely by its hazards. An impurity may be designated as non-relevant if evidence indicates no significant likelihood of its hazards being manifested in practice. 29. The relevance of impurities with additive effects with the active ingredient is assessed using the dose-additivity model. This model is not used for endpoints such as carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, teratogenicity, or eye and skin irritation and sensitization. 30. Limits for relevant impurities are determined on a case-by-case basis, taking into account expert advice from WHO or other authoritative sources. For example, limits of 10 g/kg for skin and eye irritants and 1 g/kg for sensitizing chemicals, mutagens, carcinogens, and reproductive toxicants are typical. 31. Where data are available to JMPS, a maximum acceptable limit corresponding to a negligible contribution to overall hazards will be estimated and used in preference to GHS limits. 32. For impurities posing a similar type of toxic hazard to the active ingredient (additive effects), the maximum acceptable limit adopted by JMPS normally corresponds to a concentration leading to a calculated 10% increase in the overall hazard presented by the active ingredient. 33. The determination of the maximal acceptable concentration limit for impurities without comparable numeric toxicity values will be made on a case-by-case basis. 34. The absence of an agreed and published specification guideline does not preclude submission of a proposed specification. FAO and WHO encourage the development of novel formulations addressing pest control problems. 35. For unique formulation types, the manufacturer must define the critical characteristics and provide suitably validated test methods for measuring the appropriate parameters. 36. The composition of pure active ingredient is accepted as the same in both reference material and proposed material when it is a single non-chiral compound, a single enantiomer, or a chiral compound as a racemate of an enantiomeric pair. If the pure active ingredient is a mixture, evidence must be provided to confirm the compositions are the same. 37. Physical and chemical property data available for the reference material on the pure individual isomer must be provided.
